claim: Control of voluntary limb movement is predominantly attributed to the contralateral motor cortex.
source: Control of voluntary limb movement is predominantly attributed to the contralateral motor cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction without specific experimental data from this study.

claim: Increasing evidence suggests the involvement of ipsilateral cortical networks in motor control, especially in motor tasks requiring bilateral coordination, such as locomotion.
source: However, increasing evidence suggests the involvement of ipsilateral cortical networks in this process, especially in motor tasks requiring bilateral coordination, such as locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as a general trend in the field based on existing literature.

claim: In all SCI rats, stimulation of the ipsilesional motor cortex promoted a bilateral synergy involving elevation of the contralateral foot along with ipsilateral hindlimb extension.
source: Our findings reveal that in all SCI rats, stimulation of the ipsilesional motor cortex promoted a bilateral synergy. This synergy involved the elevation of the contralateral foot along with ipsilateral hindlimb extension.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data collected in the study.

claim: In two out of seven animals, stimulation of a sub-region of the hindlimb motor cortex modulated ipsilateral hindlimb flexion.
source: Additionally, in two out of seven animals, stimulation of a sub-region of the hindlimb motor cortex modulated ipsilateral hindlimb flexion.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the experimental data.

claim: Ipsilateral cortical stimulation delivered after SCI immediately alleviated multiple locomotor and postural deficits.
source: Importantly, ipsilateral cortical stimulation delivered after SCI immediately alleviated multiple locomotor and postural deficits, and this effect persisted after ablation of the homologous motor cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data.

claim: The effect of ipsilateral cortical stimulation on alleviating locomotor and postural deficits persisted after ablation of the homologous motor cortex.
source: Importantly, ipsilateral cortical stimulation delivered after SCI immediately alleviated multiple locomotor and postural deficits, and this effect persisted after ablation of the homologous motor cortex.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the ablation experiments.

claim: Lateralization bias of cortical control is reflected anatomically by a majority of crossed corticospinal tract (CST) projections.
source: This lateralization bias is reflected (1) anatomically, by a majority of crossed corticospinal tract (CST) projections (Hicks and D'Amato, 1975)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Lateralization bias of cortical control is reflected electrophysiologically by a predominance of contralateral muscle recruitments by cortical stimulation.
source: (2) electrophysiologically, by a predominance of contralateral muscle recruitments by cortical stimulation (Kwan et al., 1978)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Lateralization bias of cortical control is reflected functionally by contralateral deficits induced by cortical lesions.
source: (3) functionally, by contralateral deficits induced by cortical lesions (Passingham et al., 1983)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Ipsilateral impairments have been reported after unilateral cortical injury or transient interference accompanied with increased cortical activity from the opposite hemisphere.
source: Ipsilateral impairments have been reported after unilateral cortical injury or transient interference (e.g. via transcranial magnetic stimulation) accompanied with increased cortical activity from the opposite hemisphere (Blasi et al., 2002; Chen et al., 1997b; Johansen-Berg et al., 2002; Jones et al., 1989; Kim et al., 2003; Marque et al., 1997; Yarosh et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The motor cortex contains a representation of both unilateral and bilateral movements in the same-side cortical hemisphere (ipsilateral).
source: While the motor cortex primarily controls movements on the opposite side of the body (contralateral), it also contains a representation of both unilateral and bilateral movements in the same-side cortical hemisphere (ipsilateral) (Aizawa et al., 1990; Ames and Churchland, 2019; Bundy et al., 2018; Cisek et al., 2003; Diedrichsen et al., 2013; Donchin et al., 1998; Ganguly et al., 2009; Ghacibeh et al., 2007; Heming et al., 2019; Kawashima et al., 1994; Merrick et al., 2022; Tinazzi and Zanette, 1998; Wisneski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Lower extremities movements and walking are associated with bilateral activity in primary sensorimotor cortices and supplementary motor areas.
source: Imaging studies have shown that lower extremities movements and walking, which require efficient bilateral coordination, are associated with bilateral activity in primary sensorimotor cortices and supplementary motor areas (Miyai et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous imaging studies.

claim: After a unilateral spinal cord injury (SCI) in rats, microstimulation delivered to the contralesional motor cortex in phase coherence with locomotion immediately alleviated contralateral hindlimb deficits.
source: In recent studies, we have shown that, after a unilateral spinal cord injury (SCI) in rats (Bonizzato and Martinez, 2021) and large spinal contusion injuries in cats (Duguay et al., 2023), microstimulation delivered to the contralesional motor cortex in phase coherence with locomotion immediately alleviated contralateral hindlimb deficits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: After large spinal contusion injuries in cats, microstimulation delivered to the contralesional motor cortex in phase coherence with locomotion immediately alleviated contralateral hindlimb deficits.
source: In recent studies, we have shown that, after a unilateral spinal cord injury (SCI) in rats (Bonizzato and Martinez, 2021) and large spinal contusion injuries in cats (Duguay et al., 2023), microstimulation delivered to the contralesional motor cortex in phase coherence with locomotion immediately alleviated contralateral hindlimb deficits.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation of the ipsilateral motor cortex in intact rats increased right step height by +119 ± 37% of the spontaneous level when synchronized with the timing of the right foot lift.
source: These alterations included an increase in right step height (+119 ± 37% of the spontaneous level, p=4E-4, t-test, phase-coherent vs. off-timing).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation in intact rats resulted in contralateral swing dominance (+22 ± 6%).
source: Additionally, the gait pattern modifications resulted in a contralateral swing dominance (i.e. significantly longer than that of the opposite limb by +22 ± 6%, p=0.03, t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation in intact rats resulted in ipsilateral stance dominance (+10 ± 3%).
source: and an ipsilateral stance dominance (+10 ± 3%, p=0.01, t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: In intact rats, phase-coherent stimulation had no discernible effects on posture across all tested rats.
source: In our investigation of the effects of modulating phase-coherent stimulation amplitudes, we observed that there were no discernible effects on posture (Figure 1C) or ipsilateral kinematics (Figure 1D) across all intact rats.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: In intact rats, phase-coherent stimulation had no discernible effects on ipsilateral kinematics across all tested rats.
source: In our investigation of the effects of modulating phase-coherent stimulation amplitudes, we observed that there were no discernible effects on posture (Figure 1C) or ipsilateral kinematics (Figure 1D) across all intact rats.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: In intact rats, increasing stimulation amplitudes resulted in linear increases in right step height (+157 ± 13%).
source: These parameters included right step height (+157 ± 13%, p=4E-5, t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: In intact rats, increasing stimulation amplitudes resulted in linear increases in flexion velocity (+107 ± 21%).
source: flexion velocity (+107 ± 21%, p=2E-4, t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: In intact rats, increasing stimulation amplitudes resulted in linear increases in swing asymmetry index (30 ± 3%).
source: and swing (30 ± 3%, p=5E-4, t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: In intact rats, increasing stimulation amplitudes resulted in linear increases in stance asymmetry index (14 ± 2%).
source: and stance (14 ± 2%, p=0.0026, t-test) asymmetry indexes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Following a left spinal hemisection at the thoracic level, rats displayed ipsilateral hindlimb motor deficits corresponding to the same side as the lesion.
source: Following a left spinal hemisection at the thoracic level (Figure 3A), rats displayed ipsilateral hindlimb motor deficits corresponding to the same side as the lesion.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental observations after injury.

claim: About 1 week after SCI, observed deficits included a lack of ipsilateral hindlimb support, as well as weaker ipsilateral flexion and extension, leading to asymmetries in the gait pattern.
source: The observed deficits included a lack of ipsilateral hindlimb support, as well as weaker ipsilateral flexion and extension, leading to asymmetries in the gait pattern (ipsilateral swing dominance 29 ± 4% and right stance dominance 16 ± 3%, Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental observations after injury with quantitative data.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation of the ipsilateral motor cortex after SCI enhanced contralateral step height.
source: Phase-coherent stimulation of the ipsilateral motor cortex (see scheme in Figure 3A) enhanced contralateral step height (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data after SCI.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation after SCI was behaviorally expressed as a bilateral synergy, characterized by a contralateral hindlimb flexion and an ipsilateral extension.
source: This effect was behaviorally expressed as a bilateral synergy, characterized by a contralateral hindlimb flexion and an ipsilateral extension.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental observations after SCI.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation after SCI led to intensified and prolonged ipsilateral weight-bearing, resulting in restoration of a balanced gait phase distribution between the ipsilateral and contralateral hindlimb.
source: Consequently, ipsilateral weight-bearing was intensified and prolonged, leading to a reversal of the motor deficits and the restoration of a balanced gait phase distribution between the ipsilateral and contralateral hindlimb (Figure 3B and C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental observations after SCI.

claim: After SCI, the most significant effects of stimulation were obtained when stimuli were delivered during the preparation and early execution of the right swing.
source: The most significant effects were obtained when stimuli were delivered during the preparation and early execution of the right swing, similar to what was observed in the intact condition (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data after SCI.

claim: After SCI, phase-coherent stimulation increased contralateral step height by +94 ± 43% compared to off-timing stimuli.
source: These strong effects included an increase in contralateral step height (+94 ± 43%, p=0.001, t-test, phase-coherent vs. off-timing stimuli)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: After SCI, phase-coherent stimulation effectively reversed the swing asymmetry deficit up to 116 ± 11% compared to intact walking.
source: as well as a counterbalance between swing (p=2E-5, t-test) and stance durations (p=0.0017, t-test) effectively reversing the asymmetry deficit up to 116 ± 11% and 115 ± 9% respectively, compared to intact walking (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: After SCI, phase-coherent stimulation effectively reversed the stance asymmetry deficit up to 115 ± 9% compared to intact walking.
source: as well as a counterbalance between swing (p=2E-5, t-test) and stance durations (p=0.0017, t-test) effectively reversing the asymmetry deficit up to 116 ± 11% and 115 ± 9% respectively, compared to intact walking (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: After SCI, when delivered during the late right or early ipsilateral stance, stimulation amplitude linearly modulated right step height (+172 ± 30%).
source: When delivered during the late right or early ipsilateral stance, stimulation amplitude linearly (VAF = 85 ± 4%) modulated right step height (+172 ± 30%, p=1E-4, t-test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: After SCI, when delivered during the late right or early ipsilateral stance, stimulation amplitude linearly modulated flexion velocity (+115 ± 22%).
source: and flexion velocity (+115 ± 22%, p=7E-4, t-test, linear fit VAF = 86 ± 4%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: After SCI, stimulation proportionally decreased the swing asymmetry index (deficit reversed up to 123 ± 10%).
source: In addition, the swing (deficit reversed up to 123 ± 10%, p=0.0018, t-test, linear fit VAF = 80 ± 7%)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: After SCI, stimulation proportionally decreased the stance asymmetry index (deficit reversed up to 125 ± 10%).
source: and stance (deficit reversed up to 125 ± 10%, p=9E-4, t-test, linear fit VAF = 86 ± 5%) asymmetry indexes proportionally decreased (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The modulation of ipsilateral hindlimb kinematics persisted even 1 month after SCI, with all effects in hindlimb extension and swing/stance asymmetry remaining consistent.
source: We confirmed that the modulation of ipsilateral hindlimb kinematics described in this experiment persisted even 1 month after SCI, with all effects in hindlimb extension and swing/stance asymmetry remaining consistent (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal experimental data.

claim: The stimulation currents needed to achieve modulation decreased over time after SCI.
source: The stimulation currents needed to achieve this modulation decreased over time (Figure 3—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal experimental data.

claim: Electrode impedances generally remained stable over time after SCI.
source: while electrode impedances generally remained stable (Figure 3—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal experimental data.

claim: Following SCI, the ipsilesional ankle extensor muscle exhibited a –72 ± 4% decrease in burst duration during spontaneous locomotion compared to intact conditions.
source: Following the injury, the ipsilesional ankle extensor muscle exhibited significant alterations during spontaneous locomotion (–72 ± 4% burst duration, p=0.007, t-test
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Following SCI, the ipsilesional ankle extensor muscle exhibited a –92 ± 2% decrease in total activation during spontaneous locomotion compared to intact conditions.
source: –92 ± 2% total activation, p=0.002, t-test, compared to intact conditions, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation after SCI reinstated the function of the ipsilesional ankle extensor muscle, leading to increased burst duration (recovered 90 ± 18% of the lost burst duration).
source: However, phase-coherent stimulation reinstated the function of this muscle, leading to increased burst duration (recovered 90 ± 18% of the lost burst duration, p=0.004, t-test, Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation after SCI reinstated the function of the ipsilesional ankle extensor muscle, leading to increased total activation (recovered 56 ± 13% of the total activation).
source: and total activation (recovered 56 ± 13% of the total activation, p=0.014, t-test, Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The degree of improvement in ipsilesional ankle extensor muscle function was linearly correlated with the applied stimulus amplitude (VAF=[84±7, 84±10]%).
source: with the degree of improvement linearly correlated with the applied stimulus amplitude (VAF=[84±7, 84±10]%).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data showing linear correlation.

claim: After SCI, rats displayed a low posture due to the loss of weight acceptance on their ipsilateral hindlimb, and the severity of these postural deficits depended on the SCI severity.
source: After the injury, rats displayed a low posture due to the loss of weight acceptance on their ipsilateral hindlimb, and the severity of these postural deficits depended on the SCI severity (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental observations after SCI.

claim: During recovery, postural compensation occurred, leading to a notably elevated posture 1 month after SCI.
source: However, during the recovery process, postural compensation occurred, leading to a notably elevated posture 1 month after SCI (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from longitudinal experimental observations.

claim: Phase-coherent stimulation administered in the early ipsilateral stance phase immediately alleviated postural deficits 1 week after injury, and the iliac crest height increased proportionally with higher stimulation amplitudes.
source: Phase-coherent stimulation, administered in the early ipsilateral stance phase, immediately alleviated postural deficits 1 week after injury, and the iliac crest height increased proportionally with higher stimulation amplitudes (p=0.03, t-test, VAF = 76 ± 9%, Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: 5 days after SCI, the ipsilateral corticospinal transmission decreased by approximately –90 ± 7%.
source: Initially, the injury led to a substantial decrease in corticospinal transmission on both sides: 5 days after the injury, the ipsilateral (left motor cortex to left hindlimb) and contralateral (left motor cortex to right hindlimb) transmission decreased by approximately –90 ± 7% and –53±13% (p=[2E-4, 5E-4], Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 6B), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: 5 days after SCI, the contralateral corticospinal transmission decreased by approximately –53±13%.
source: Initially, the injury led to a substantial decrease in corticospinal transmission on both sides: 5 days after the injury, the ipsilateral (left motor cortex to left hindlimb) and contralateral (left motor cortex to right hindlimb) transmission decreased by approximately –90 ± 7% and –53±13% (p=[2E-4, 5E-4], Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 6B), respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: The size of the contralateral map substantially increased by 2 weeks after SCI (+264 ± 20%) and remained consolidated 8 weeks after injury (+250 ± 21%).
source: The size of the contralateral map (i.e. the number of responding sites on the implanted array) substantially increased by 2 weeks (+264 ± 20%) and remained consolidated 8 weeks after injury (+250 ± 21%, p=2E-4, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Over time, the representation of ipsilateral hindlimb movements significantly increased compared to the intact condition (+115 ± 26%).
source: Over time, the representation of ipsilateral hindlimb movements significantly increased compared to the intact condition (+115 ± 26%, p=0.002, Wilcoxon signed-rank test, Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Between weeks 1 and 2 after SCI, 91 ± 22% of the overall postural correction occurred.
source: Between weeks 1 and 2, 91 ± 22% of the overall postural correction (Figures 5B and 6C)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Between weeks 1 and 2 after SCI, 71 ± 2% of the overall locomotor score recovery occurred.
source: and 71 ± 2% of the overall locomotor score recovery occurred (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: Between weeks 1 and 2 after SCI, 83 ± 7% of the increment in size of the ipsilateral map took place.
source: Furthermore, 83 ± 7% of the increment in size of the ipsilateral map took place within the same time interval (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data.

claim: For each individual rat, the trend of locomotor score improvement measured during the first 3 weeks after SCI correlated with both ipsilateral (VAF: 84 ± 3%) and contralateral (VAF: 82 ± 4%) hindlimb representations in the left cortex.
source: For each individual rat, the trend of locomotor score improvement measured during the first 3 weeks after SCI correlated with both ipsilateral (VAF: 84 ± 3%) and contralateral (VAF: 82 ± 4%) hindlimb representations in the left cortex.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data showing correlation.

claim: For any given day post-injury, the size of the left motor map across rats did not predict locomotor performance measured in an open field (VAF was 3 ± 2% for ipsilateral transmission and 8 ± 4% for contralateral transmission).
source: However, it is important to note that for any given day post-injury, the size of the left motor map across rats did not predict locomotor performance measured in an open field. The VAF was 3 ± 2% for ipsilateral transmission and 8 ± 4% for contralateral transmission (Figure 6E–G)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data showing lack of correlation.

claim: The size of the left motor map did not correlate with lesion size.
source: Additionally, the size of the left motor map did not correlate with lesion size (Figure 6F)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing lack of correlation.

claim: The return of distal representations within the ipsilateral motor maps correlated with the recovery of fine motor control 3 weeks after SCI.
source: When assessing the correlation between ipsilateral motor maps and skilled locomotor performance on the ladder task, we found that the return of distal representations within the ipsilateral motor maps correlated with the recovery of fine motor control 3 weeks after SCI (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing correlation.

claim: The correlation between distal representations within the ipsilateral motor maps and fine motor control disappeared 4 weeks after SCI.
source: This correlation disappeared 4 weeks after SCI and was not observed when including proximal movements.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing loss of correlation over time.

claim: In two out of seven rats tested for phase-coherent stimulation, stimulation of specific array sites within a medial area of the hindlimb motor cortex preferentially evoked ipsilateral flexor responses.
source: However, in our study, we observed a unique motor response in two out of the seven rats tested for phase-coherent stimulation (Figure 7A, Supplementary file 1). Specifically, in these two rats, tested 2 weeks after SCI, stimulation of specific array sites within a medial area of the hindlimb motor cortex (1.1 mm mediolateral from bregma, Figure 7D) preferentially evoked ipsilateral flexor responses
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: In rat#1, 3 channels showed 271 ± 36% ipsilateral dominance, while the rest of responding channels showed 43 ± 4% ipsilateral dominance.
source: (Figure 7B–D, rat#1: 3 channels with 271 ± 36% ipsilateral dominance, rest of responding channels 43 ± 4%, p=0.003, Wilcoxon rank-sum test
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: In rat#2, 6 channels showed 452 ± 87% ipsilateral dominance, while all other channels showed 18 ± 4% ipsilateral dominance.
source: rat#2: 6 channels 452 ± 87%, all others 18 ± 4%, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p=2E-4).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Stimuli delivered during the late ipsilateral stance resulted in kinematic modulation: step height increased by +133 ± 18% in rat#1 and +99 ± 23% in rat#2.
source: Stimuli delivered during the late ipsilateral stance resulted in kinematic modulation: step height (+133 ± 18, +99 ± 23%, p=[1E-4,0.001], Wilcoxon rank-sum test)
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: Stimuli delivered during the late ipsilateral stance resulted in flexion velocity increases of +46 ± 19% in rat#1 and +101 ± 19% in rat#2.
source: and flexion velocity (+46 ± 19, +101 ± 19%, p=[0.01, 1E-4], Wilcoxon rank-sum test) increased linearly (rat#1: VAF=(90, 91)%, rat#2: VAF=(95, 86)%) with greater stimulation amplitudes (Figure 7E, Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: As a result of ipsilateral flexion modulation, dragging was immediately alleviated (–46±6, –100%).
source: As a result, dragging was immediately alleviated (–46±6, –100%, p=[1E-6, 7E-4], Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data with statistical significance.

claim: In three rats with combined thoracic unilateral SCI and surgical ablation of the contralateral motor cortex, modulation of leg extension was readily obtained through phase-coherent ipsilateral cortical neurostimulation 1 week after SCI.
source: In three rats we combined thoracic unilateral SCI with a surgical ablation of the contralateral motor cortex (Figure 8A) to determine whether contralateral cortical networks are necessary to ipsilateral hindlimb modulation. In all three rats, modulation of leg extension was readily obtained through phase-coherent ipsilateral cortical neurostimulation 1 week after SCI.
evidence: This is a finding from the ablation experiments.

claim: All three rats with contralateral motor cortex ablation displayed postural deficits that were immediately alleviated by phase-coherent stimulation of the ipsilesional motor cortex.
source: All three rats displayed postural deficits that were immediately alleviated by phase-coherent stimulation of the ipsilesional motor cortex (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the ablation experiments.

claim: In six intact rats, long-train stimulation of one motor cortex evoked locomotor-like rhythms characterized by bilateral alternated whole-leg movements.
source: In six intact rats, we found that long-train stimulation of one motor cortex evoked locomotor-like rhythms (Figure 9A and B, Figure 9—video 1), characterized by bilateral alternated whole-leg movements.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: 1 week after unilateral hemisection SCI, in half of the tested rats with more severe injuries and lower ladder crossing performance, bilateral alternated locomotor-like rhythms did not emerge immediately after injury.
source: Subsequently, we assessed whether 1 week after unilateral hemisection SCI, long-train stimulation of the ipsilesional motor cortex could induce bilateral rhythms. We observed that in half of the tested rats with more severe injuries and lower ladder crossing performance, bilateral alternated locomotor-like rhythms did not emerge immediately after injury.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data after SCI.

claim: By week 2 or 3 post-injury, bilateral alternated rhythms returned in rats with more severe injuries.
source: However, by week 2 or 3 post-injury, these bilateral rhythms returned (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data after SCI.

claim: The remaining three rats with less severe injuries exhibited bilateral alternated hindlimb rhythms when receiving ipsilesional cortical stimulation as early as 1 week after injury.
source: In contrast, the remaining three rats with less severe injuries exhibited bilateral alternated hindlimb rhythms when receiving ipsilesional cortical stimulation as early as 1 week after injury (Figure 9D).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data after SCI.

claim: Ketamine sedation suppressed rhythmic hindlimb responses in four intact rats.
source: To illustrate the well-known absence of rhythmic hindlimb activity after ketamine sedation, we tested and recorded four intact rats before and after ketamine injection, confirming the suppression of rhythmic hindlimb responses (Figure 9E–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data confirming known effects of ketamine.

claim: The ipsilesional motor cortex can activate and influence bilateral lumbar synergistic networks through descending connections spared by the injury.
source: Thus, the ipsilesional motor cortex can activate and influence bilateral lumbar synergistic networks through descending connections spared by the injury.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The acute expression of bilateral synergy (1 week after injury) is compatible with an adaptive or compensatory upregulation of pre-existing functional networks after SCI.
source: We propose that the acute expression of this bilateral synergy (1 week after injury) is compatible with an adaptive or compensatory upregulation of pre-existing functional networks after SCI.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Rapid onset of postural compensation is displayed behaviorally by rats during the same timeframe as the acute expression of bilateral synergy.
source: Rapid onset of postural compensation is also displayed behaviorally by rats during the same timeframe (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental observations.

claim: After a unilateral cortical injury, plastic changes are observed in the opposite hemisphere.
source: After a unilateral cortical injury, plastic changes are observed in the opposite hemisphere (Axelson et al., 2013; Dancause et al., 2005; Mansoori et al., 2014; Rehme et al., 2012; Shimizu et al., 2002; Strens et al., 2003; Witte et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Laterally unbalanced SCIs induce dynamic changes in the contralesional and ipsilesional motor cortex, which may participate in functional recovery or compensation mechanisms.
source: Laterally unbalanced SCIs induce dynamic changes in the contralesional and ipsilesional motor cortex, which may participate in functional recovery or compensation mechanisms (Bonizzato and Martinez, 2021; Brown and Martinez, 2018; Brown and Martinez, 2021; Ghosh et al., 2010; Ghosh et al., 2009; Nishimura et al., 2007; Schmidlin et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In all rats, corticospinal transmission significantly decreased after injury, independently from the subject-specific size of the injury.
source: We tracked the progression of motor representation of both hindlimbs in the ipsilesional motor cortex and found that in all rats, corticospinal transmission significantly decreased after injury (Figure 6B), independently from the subject-specific size of the injury (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The loss of excitability quickly recovered within 2 weeks after SCI.
source: The loss of excitability quickly recovered within 2 weeks (Figure 6B)
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data.

claim: The subject-specific size of cortical motor maps did not correlate with the behaviorally expressed global motor performance measured in an open field.
source: However, the subject-specific size of cortical motor maps did not correlate with the behaviorally expressed global motor performance measured in an open field (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental data showing lack of correlation.

claim: Recovery of hindlimb movement after SCI may be more tightly connected to changes in the contralateral cortical motor representation rather than the ipsilateral cortical motor representation.
source: Comparison of these two results suggested that recovery of hindlimb movement after SCI may be more tightly connected to changes in the contralateral cortical motor representation rather than the ipsilateral cortical motor representation, even in fully lateralized thoracic injuries, which disproportionally affect the crossed projections from the contralateral motor cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison of current and previous findings.

claim: The return of bilateral corticospinal transmission from the ipsilesional motor cortex after SCI is an important excitatory drive that supports bilateral skilled hindlimb movement.
source: These combined results suggested that, although not a precise predictor of motor performance, the return of bilateral corticospinal transmission from the ipsilesional motor cortex after SCI is an important excitatory drive that supports bilateral skilled hindlimb movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined experimental findings.

claim: The two rats exhibiting ipsilateral hindlimb flexion modulation had arrays positioned at precisely the same brain coordinates ([1.1 mm posterior, 1.1 mm lateral] from bregma) and depth (1.5 mm).
source: These rats had arrays positioned at precisely the same brain coordinates ([1.1 mm posterior, 1.1 .mm lateral] from bregma) and depth (1.5 mm).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The lesion profiles of the two rats exhibiting ipsilateral hindlimb flexion modulation were substantially different.
source: However, their lesion profiles were substantially different (see Figure 2A, purple stars and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental observations.

claim: The remaining five rats used to test immediate modulation of movement under cortical stimulation did not exhibit ipsilateral hindlimb flexion, despite having variable lesion profiles.
source: Interestingly, the remaining five rats (see Figure 2A, blue stars) used to test immediate modulation of movement under cortical stimulation did not exhibit ipsilateral hindlimb flexion, despite having variable lesion profiles.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental observations.

claim: No relationship was found between spared pathways on the lesioned side and the capacity to neuroprosthetically achieve ipsilateral flexion modulation.
source: Thus, we did not find a relationship between spared pathways on the lesioned side and the capacity to neuroprosthetically achieve ipsilateral flexion modulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental observations.

claim: Unilateral cortical drive can activate spinal locomotor circuits, leading to the generation of alternated 'air-stepping' in awake rats even in the absence of cutaneous interaction with a ground surface.
source: While afferent inputs are known to play a crucial role in spinal locomotion (Alluin et al., 2015; Barthélemy et al., 2007; Sławińska et al., 2012), our study demonstrates that unilateral cortical drive can activate spinal locomotor circuits, leading to the generation of alternated 'air-stepping' in awake rats even in the absence of cutaneous interaction with a ground surface.
